Help me make an original mobile game "highlight moment" animation: [Subject, e.g.: opening a treasure chest / rank promotion / achievement unlocked / Boss drop / character level-up].
Make it a single-file web page (HTML + CSS + JS) that can be opened directly and plays in full with one click, with an effect that matches the result / reward presentations of commercial mobile games.

[Worldview and Style]
- Original art; do not imitate any existing game's IP, characters or logo.
- Cartoon mobile-game style: highly saturated colours, a uniform dark outline (e.g. #1A1033), rounded, chunky shapes.
- Colours upgrade with the tier: [tier ladder, e.g.: common green → rare blue → epic purple → legendary gold]. With each tier up, switch the main colour, the light-effect colour and the background tone.
- The title uses a round, fat game font (such as Titan One / Lilita One), with a black outline and a drop shadow; the text "slams" into the screen letter by letter, with a bounce-back.

[Main Object: Make It True 3D]
- Model it with Three.js; do not use flat SVG textures. It needs thickness, bevels, and structural details appropriate to the subject (plank seams, rivets, edge trim, gem facets, latches, etc.); details like plank seams must be built from real geometry, not by pasting black lines.
- Shade it with cartoon banding (MeshToonMaterial with a 3 to 4 step gradient map), with three lights: key light, sky light, and a tier-coloured rim light.
- Draw outlines with post-process edge detection: render a normal map plus a depth map, then draw the lines with a shader. Thick for the outer silhouette, thin where parts meet, with consistent thickness throughout; also do 1.5x supersampling and multisample anti-aliasing.
  Do not use the "slightly enlarged black back-face" outline method, because its thickness is uneven and it breaks at corners.
  Loosen the depth-test threshold, and detect seams mainly with normals, otherwise fine diagonal streaks appear on surfaces seen at a slant.
- Moving parts must move realistically, e.g. the chest lid flips open around its hinge, and a medal rotates around its vertical axis.
- At idle, the subject slowly turns left and right so the sides and thickness can be seen, while bobbing slightly up and down; there must be a soft shadow under its feet that varies with height.

[If the Screen Has 2D Illustrations (card faces, reward icons, characters)]
- Three-layer cartoon shading: base colour, blocky shadow colour, and highlight colour; do not use just a single gradient.
- Lines of differing weight: thick for the outer outline, thin for internal structure lines.
- Each character or object should have its own expression and pose; do not let everything share the same face.
- Draw a drop shadow beneath the feet so the subject "stands" in the scene; vary the background pattern by attribute, and do not use the same radial lines for everything.

[Pacing of the Presentation: Five Phases, None Optional]
1. Ready: the subject idles and floats, shakes every few seconds to hint it can be clicked, and a "Tap" prompt is shown at the bottom.
2. Level-up: with each click, the subject jumps up, spins once in the air, squashes on landing and springs back; at the same time it switches to the next tier's colour, flashes, bursts out a ring of particles, and the title updates.
3. Charge-up (about 1 second): the subject shakes more and more violently, light leaks through the seams, particles around it are sucked toward the centre, and the sound pitch keeps rising; at the last moment it squashes down hard.
4. Burst: a flash of bloom white spreading outward from the burst point, screen shake, the camera pushing forward, multiple layers of shockwaves, slender streaks of light shooting out, glittering star points, and coins and gems (spinning). Bursts at high tiers must be clearly stronger. Confetti is used only once, at the climax; do not fill the screen with confetti.
5. Reveal and settlement:
   - The reward card flies out of the subject along an arc, landing with overshoot and a wobbling finish, and the numbers count up by rolling.
   - Rare items get a rainbow flowing-light border and a "NEW!" corner badge.
   - After tapping to claim, coins and gems fly along Bezier curves into the balance at the top right, and the balance bounces each time one arrives.

[Reveal Stage: Let the Hero Own the Screen]
- When revealing the highest rarity, other elements retract or fade out, and behind it a clean gradient backdrop plus slowly rotating soft light replaces the scene; do not let the hero sit on a cluttered background.
- When the backdrop appears, hide the other 3D objects in the scene, otherwise the post-process outline will draw their silhouette lines on the backdrop.
- The hero's outer glow must sit behind the subject and only spill from the edges; it must not cover the front of the subject and wash it out into a patch of white.
- You may add a ring of stardust trails circling the hero, but the orbit must lie entirely outside the hero's silhouette and must not sweep across the front of the subject.

[Light Effects: Must Be Soft, No Hard Edges]
- Background rays: use a conic-gradient with gradient transitions, not blocks with sharp edges; layer 2 to 3 layers of light with different densities and rotation speeds.
- Light pillar: 5 to 7 blurred beams fanning out, each flickering slightly in brightness; add a soft glowing core at the root, with light dust slowly drifting upward inside the light.
- Flash: a radial bloom outward from the burst point (mix-blend-mode: screen), with intensity not exceeding 0.8, and no full-screen pure-white overexposure.
- Particles: each spark carries a low-opacity outer halo; shockwaves use three layers of stroke (wide and faint, medium, thin and bright).

[Materials and UI]
- Frames, nameplates and buttons need a sense of material: brushed-metal gradients, bevel light that is bright at top left and dark at bottom right, and inner shadows; swap the inlays by rarity (steel rivets → silver frame with gems → gold frame with diamond and a small crown).
- Do not cram small numeric text onto small cards; put detailed values into the info panel shown at the reveal, where the numbers roll upward and pop out a "▲+value".
- Textures drawn on Canvas must have a resolution at least 1.5 times the largest on-screen display size, otherwise they blur when scaled up.

[Animation Principles]
- Orchestrate with GSAP timelines. All motion must have squash and stretch, overshoot and elastic bounce-back; nothing at constant speed.
- Write the particle system yourself with Canvas 2D: gravity, drag, lifetime, additive blending, and three kinds of motion: "sucked in", "curved flight" and "orbiting".
- Do not use CSS 3D perspective to flip large elements, because when scaling up with a side flip they get projected into a flat plane that fills the screen; do all 3D flips in WebGL.
- For all looping tweens of the "shake" and "breathing" type, cancel them first and then zero them out on a state switch, to avoid them finishing one frame after the stop command and setting the value back.

[Sound Effects]
- All synthesized in real time with Web Audio, no audio files: jump, landing, level-up chord, charge-up rising tone, explosion low frequency plus noise, pop, counting ticks, coin clinks, victory fanfare.
- Initialize audio only on the first click; put a mute toggle at the top right.

[UI and Engineering]
- Top HUD: mode switch, coin and gem balances, mute button.
- It must also work at phone width; respect the "reduce motion" setting (turn off screen shake, reduce particles).
- The animation state machine must be rigorous: ignore clicks while an animation is playing, with no swallowed clicks or confused states.
- Target 60fps. The first time it opens it must already be a complete idle screen, not blank.

[Self-Check Before Delivery]
Take one screenshot each at the charge-up, burst, reveal and settlement moments, and check them one by one:
- Is the hero blocked by glow, particles or text?
- Is it overexposed into a patch of white?
- Is the background cluttered, and are there any outline lines that give the game away?
- Is the small text legible?
- After settlement, is anything still shaking when it shouldn't be moving?

Finally, tell me: the duration of each phase, and which parameters can be adjusted to tune the intensity of the presentation.
